name: Emeka Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Emeka. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brightline, a contractor the electricity company hires for pole replacements and new-build connections. So most days we're on a housing estate going up near the motorway, setting new poles, running cable and hooking up show homes, or out swapping old poles on a programme list. I like seeing a street go from mud to lights on. What wears me out is that my contract gets renewed every April, and you never quite know.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my younger brother Chidi, who's at college doing plumbing. I help with his fees and send a bit to our mum each month. So between that and rent, I've got under a month saved. I use AI now and then, mostly to check my maths on cable sizes or to write emails to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, most new things are oversold. I'd say it on the crew van and not think much more. I don't really post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same old April worry. My contract's been renewed four years running, but my firm lost a bid last year in the next county and twelve lads went. Nothing to do with AI, just the bidding game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working hard so I'm on the keep list, and try to build two months of savings before April. I'd also keep helping Chidi finish his course, because a second trade in the house is good for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the usual kind. Not panic, just that spring feeling every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you do when those twelve lads went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lent one of them, Ade, a hundred to cover his phone bill. And I worked every Saturday for two months, in case they were watching who was keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if April went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the money to mum first, which I'd hate. Then the gym. Chidi's fees I'd keep, that's the future.

I'd say that on the **crew van** and move on.
think: It's the same old **April worry** about my contract renewal.
Brightline **lost a bid** last year and twelve lads went.
do: Work hard to stay on the **keep list** at Brightline.
Build **two months** of savings before April.
Keep paying **Chidi's fees** so he finishes plumbing.
S0.quote: My contract's been renewed four years running, but my firm lost a bid last year in the next county and twelve lads went.
fieldNote: His insecurity comes from **yearly contracts**, not AI.
He supports his **brother and mum**, which stretches his thin cushion.
He shows loyalty, lending a laid-off **colleague** money.

steps.text: Work Saturdays so Brightline keeps him on at renewal

Keep paying Chidi's plumbing college fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so we might as well get good at it. I'd tell the lads to learn the new planning tools if Brightline brings them in. Moaning won't stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it squeezes contractors hard. If the electricity company uses AI to plan and price every job, they'll push our rates down, and my firm will cut crews to win bids. I'm mid-level, not the best, so I could be one of the ones to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever app Brightline uses, once I'd seen the foreman use it. I'd start an evening course for a domestic electrician licence, so I could wire houses if the line work dries up. And I'd stop sending as much to mum for a year, which I'd explain to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why domestic electrics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because houses always need rewiring, and people pay cash for small jobs. It's a fallback. Chidi and I could even work together one day, plumbing and electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum take getting less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say keep it, look after yourself. But I'd feel bad. I'd still send something every month, even fifty.

say: AI is **coming**, so we might as well get good at it.
**Moaning** won't stop it, so learn the planning tools.
think: AI pricing would **squeeze contractors** and push rates down.
As an **average worker**, I could be one of the ones to go.
do: Learn Brightline's **new app** once the foreman uses it.
Start an evening course for a **domestic electrician** licence.
Cut what I send **mum** for a year.

fieldNote: He sees **contractor pricing** as the real AI risk to him.

He's **realistic** about being average, which sharpens his worry.

steps.text: Learn Brightline's planning app after watching the foreman use it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need someone sensible in charge, government and companies working together so it's not chaos. I'd not be on the barricades, but I'd want a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, contractors go first. By 2028 the whole planning and bidding side is AI, and by 2031 robots set poles. Brightline would shrink to almost nothing, and I'd be 32 with my brother and mum relying on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rush the domestic licence, nights and weekends. I'd do small house jobs for cash as soon as I'm licensed. And I'd tell Chidi to finish fast and get on the tools, because plumbing robots might be further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the April letter, but for everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would house wiring be safe from robots by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe a bit longer, because every house is different. It's a guess. But it's the best one I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your mum's money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It stops for a while, honestly. I'd tell her straight. My mum raised three of us on a cleaner's wage, so she knows how it goes when money stops.

say: We need **government and companies** working together so it isn't chaos.
I'd not be on the barricades, but I'd want a **plan**.
think: At **32**, with Chidi and mum relying on me, I'd have little to fall back on.

Do small **house jobs** for cash once licensed.
Push Chidi to **finish fast** and start working.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the April letter but for **everyone** at once.
S2.quote: My mum raised three of us on a cleaner's wage, so she knows how it goes when money stops.
fieldNote: He expects **Brightline** to shrink almost to nothing within a few years.
He admits the **domestic work** fallback is only a guess about robots.

steps.text: Finish the domestic electrician licence on nights and weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort it, so let's not panic. Get the training going, keep the crews working while we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still tough but doable. Planning goes in 2031, robots in 2034. That's seven years of line work if Brightline holds on, and time for my licence and some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the domestic licence in the first two years and start weekend jobs. I'd save two months by 2028. And I'd look at whether Chidi and I could set up together, electrics and plumbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a getting-on-with-it way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Brightline before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the weekend work was steady. I'm not leaving a wage for a maybe. Once I've seen the weekend work go steady, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you two call the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Garcia Brothers, probably. Mum would like that. We've joked about it for years.

fieldNote: He **waits for proof** before leaving his job, true to his steady style.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair runway. I'd tell the young lads to get a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I'm least scared of. By 2039 I'd be 40, with maybe a small business going with Chidi. The line work might shrink but I'd have something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the licence slowly, build savings, and start weekend work when it makes sense. I'd keep at Brightline as long as they renew me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the contracts. The robots feel far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust you'll actually do it slowly, not leave it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'd set a date. I'm not the type to put things off forever, but I need to see others do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would worry less. Chidi would have a partner. That's not bad.

I'd tell the **young lads** to get a second trade.
think: It's the one I'm **least scared** of.

do: Do the **licence** slowly and set a date.

fieldNote: The **decade** turns his fear into a slow plan.

steps.text: Set a date to finish the domestic electrician licence

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Contractors go first and fast. What would help is training grants for a second trade and some rules on how contracts get bid, so it's not just the cheapest robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about families. People think of us as single lads, but plenty of us send money home. If the wage goes, it's not just one person.

headlineQuote: People think of us as single lads, but plenty of us send money home.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** lineworker for **Brightline**, a contractor on new-build and pole jobs.
He shares a flat with his brother **Chidi** and sends money to his mum.
His contract is renewed **every April**, a stress that comes before any AI.
He adopts tools **once proven** and plans a second trade in domestic electrics.
He's **uneasy** in calm pictures and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because contractors like Brightline would go first.
whatWouldHelp: **Training grants** for a second trade and fairer **bidding rules**.
